thesis: NEAR's long-term case rests on an ecosystem that keeps what it builds. If projects launched on NEAR survive longer each year, and more are born than buried, the chain is compounding real builders, not renting them with incentives.

claims.title: Newer cohorts survive longer
claims.claim: The most recent cohort with a full year of data keeps more of its members alive at 12 months than the oldest cohort did.
claims.kill: Latest cohort's 12-month survival is below the oldest cohort's.
claims.why: Direction matters more than level. A chain can start with a weak first cohort and still be compounding if each cohort outlasts the last.

claims.title: Not just a graveyard
claims.claim: Of everything born more than a year ago, a meaningful share is still alive today.
claims.kill: Fewer than 10% of entities older than 12 months are alive.
claims.why: A deliberately lenient bar. For reference, about a third of US business establishments are still operating ten years after opening (BLS).

claims.title: Births outpace deaths
claims.claim: Over the latest year whose deaths are final, more projects were born than died.
claims.kill: Deaths exceed births over that year.
claims.why: Zero is the natural line. Below it, the population of living projects is shrinking.

claims.title: Not one-hit wonders
claims.claim: A typical project lives at least six months before going quiet.
claims.kill: Median lifetime across all cohorts is under 6 months.
claims.why: Six months is two death windows (2 x 90 days). A project that cannot outlast that never really operated.

death_gap_why: 90 days is one quarter. A DAO that files no proposal for a whole quarter is treated as stopped.
